newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Wall St leads European stocks to records.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wall St leads European stocks to records.

text.p: Leading European share markets climbed to record levels again on Tuesday, propelled by Wall Street's seemingly unstoppable bull run, but a British central bank warning on inflation capped London's surge.
By contrast, the dollar stabilised as Japanese officials tried to soothe foreign exchange markets after their efforts last week to talk down the U.S. currency proved unexpectedly effective.
European investors, especially in Britain and Germany, are increasingly uneasy as share markets keep on rising and they believe a correction is now only a matter of time.

But Wall Street's overnight surge was simply too big to ignore. The Dow Jones Industrial average jumped 123.22 points or 1.72 percent to a record 7,292.75 as investors gambled that the U.S. Federal Reserve would not raise interest rates at a policy meeting on May 20.

In London, the FTSE 100 index climbed for the 11th consecutive session to an intraday record of 4,720.3 points. But the Bank of England then issued a reminder that the issue of interest rates was not yet settled, on this side of the Atlantic at least.
In its quarterly inflation report, the central bank said a further tightening of monetary policy was needed if Britain was to hit its its inflation target of 2.5 percent or less in the medium term.

The report was closely watched as the new Labour government last week gave the Bank of England the power to set interest rates. In his last act under the old rules, finance minister Gordon Brown pushed up rates by 0.25 percentage points last week to preempt inflation.

"(This is) certainly not as market-friendly as we were expecting," said David Coleman of CIBC Wood Gundy. "The surprise is that they are still calling for another tightening of policy before seeing the effects of the last one."
The report stopped the FTSE in its tracks and by late morning it had slipped to 4,716.9 points, still up 47.3 points or 1.01 percent on the day.
Since April 15, the FTSE has risen over 300 points or 10 percent as investors took a more relaxed view about inflationary pressures and rising interest rates on both sides of the Atlantic.

Faced with such a rapid rise, traders believe the euphoria will not last. "This market is overbought and needs to come down. All it will take is a big one-day drop on Wall Street to set things in motion," one trader said.

Markets believe the U.S. economy is enjoying strong growth without the inflationary pressures which accompanied past upswings. This means the Fed might not feel the need to raise rates for a second time this year on May 20.
But every week brings more U.S. economic data which can rapidly change perceptions.
This week investors are awaiting the April producer price index due on Wednesday and the April retail sales report, due at 1230 GMT on Thursday.

Paris was the strongest of the leading markets in percentage terms with the CAC 40 index of blue chips up 36.21 points or 1.34 percent at 2,729.30, albeit below the all time high of 2,736.71 set in March.
The French market has worries of its own with parliamentary elections scheduled for May 25 and June 1.
Two overnight opinion polls by Louis Harris and and BVA gave a lead to the centre-right government coalition, which investors believe to be more friendly to business than the opposition Socialists.
These polls follow a weekend Sofres study which gave the coalition a comfortable lead after a series of polls which indicated that the race would be tightly contested.
On the German markets the DAX index also climbed to an intraday record but at a more modest pace. By late morning it was up 14.37 points or 0.4 percent at 3,589.74.

Prices were below all-time highs set in non-bourse electronic trade as investors grew nervous at the dizzy levels. Deutsche Telekom fell 1.04 marks to 40.15 marks on profit taking after the company announced a group net profit of 1.8 billion marks ($1.1 billion), a figure which analysts said was better than expected.

The dollar was stable against the yen and mark, helped by calls from Japanese officials for calmer foreign exchange markets. It was at 118.88 yen after dipping to its lowest level in almost four months on Monday at 117.50.

"This has been such a choppy, rumour-driven market in recent days that the market seems to have stalled itself until a more concrete fix on events feeds through," said Julian Jessop, international economist at Nikko Europe.

Japanese ministry of finance officials precipitated the biggest one-week dollar/yen fall since 1989 last week by warning the markets about possible intervention to prevent further yen weakness. This combined with talk of a Japanese interest rate rise to send the dollar into tailspin.
But earlier on Tuesday, Japanese finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said he expected foreign exchange markets to settle down soon at an appropriate level.
Against the mark, the dollar was little changed from Monday just below the psychological 1.70 level at 1.6986 compared with 1.7035 late on Monday.
STOCK PRICES AT 1045 GMT
London's FTSE 100 was at 4,716.9 points, up 47.3 points or 1.01 percent.
The Paris CAC-40 index was up 36.21 points or 1.34 percent at 2,729.30.
Frankfurt's DAX index was up 14.37 points (0.4 percent) at 3,589.74.
CURRENCIES AT 1045 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.6986 marks compared with 1.7035 late in Europe on Monday and 118.88 yen versus 118.86.
PRECIOUS METALS AT 1045 GMT
Gold was fixed in the morning at $347.30 an ounce after losing at $348.75 in London on Monday. Silver was down four cents at $4.84. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
